en: Thus have I heard: the Upāli Sutta, the fifty-sixth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.
Now at that time, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was residing at Nāḷandā together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī, having wandered for alms in Nāḷandā, returned from his almsround after his meal.
He went to the Pāvārika mango grove where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. As Dīgha Tapassī the Nigaṇṭha stood there, the Blessed One said to him:
“There are seats available, Tapassī; if you wish, please sit down.”
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī:
“But, Tapassī, how many kinds of actions does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe for the performance of evil action, for the undertaking of evil action?”
“Friend Gotama, it is not the custom of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta to prescribe ‘action, action’;
rather, friend Gotama, it is the custom of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta to prescribe ‘the rod, the rod.
“But, Tapassī, how many kinds of rods does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe for the performance of evil action, for the occurrence of evil action?”
“Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta prescribes three rods for the performance of evil action, for the occurrence of evil action;
namely, the bodily rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod.
“But, Tapassī, is the bodily rod one thing, the verbal rod another, and the mental rod yet another?”
“Friend Gotama, the bodily rod is one thing, the verbal rod another, and the mental rod is yet another.
“But, Tapassī, of these three rods thus analyzed and thus distinguished,
which rod does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe as the most blameworthy for the performance of evil action?”
"In the commission of evil action— whether it be the bodily rod, the verbal rod, or the mental rod?
"Of these three rods, friend Gotama, thus analyzed and thus distinguished,
the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta proclaims the bodily rod to be the most blameworthy for the performance of evil action."
“Compared to the occurrence of evil karma, neither the rod of speech nor the rod of mind is so [significant],” [he said].
“Do you say, Tapassī, ‘the rod of the body’?
“I say, friend Gotama, ‘the rod of the body’.”
“Do you say, Tapassī, ‘the bodily rod’?
“I do say, friend Gotama, ‘the bodily rod’.
“Do you say, Tapassī, ‘the bodily rod’?”
“I say, friend Gotama, that there is a bodily rod.
Thus the Blessed One made the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī maintain his position up to the third time regarding this point of discussion.
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī said this to the Blessed One:
“But you, friend Gotama, how many punishments do you prescribe for the performance of evil action, for the occurrence of evil action?
“Tāpasī, it is not the custom of the Tathāgata to prescribe ‘punishment, punishment’;
rather, Tāpasī, it is the custom of the Tathāgata to prescribe ‘action, action.’”
“But you, friend Gotama, how many kinds of actions do you prescribe for the performance of evil action, for the occurrence of evil action?
“Tapassī, I prescribe three kinds of actions for the performance of evil action, for the occurrence of evil action; namely:
bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.”
“But, friend Gotama, is bodily action one thing, verbal action another, and mental action yet another?
“Bodily action is indeed one thing, Tapassī, verbal action is another, and mental action is yet another.
“But, friend Gotama, regarding these three kinds of action thus analyzed and thus distinguished...”
"Which action did he prescribe as the most blameworthy for the performance of evil karma, for the occurrence of evil karma—
whether it be bodily action, verbal action, or mental action? "Tapassī,
of these three types of actions thus analyzed and thus distinguished," [he replied].
“I declare that mental action is more blameworthy for the performance of evil karma and for the occurrence of evil karma than is bodily action, and than is verbal action.
“Friend Gotama, you say ‘mental action’?”
“Mental action, Tapassī, I say.
“Do you say, friend Gotama, that it is mental action?
“Mental action, Tapassī, I say.”
“Friend Gotama, do you say ‘mental action’?
“I say ‘mental action,’ Tapassī.
Thus, after having established the Blessed One in this line of discussion up to the third time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī rose from his seat and approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Now at that time, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was seated together with a large assembly of householders, an assembly headed by Upāli and consisting of women from Bālaka.
The Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta saw the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī coming from afar;
having seen him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī:
“Come now, ascetic, where have you come from so early in the day?
“Indeed, venerable sir, I have come here from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
“But did you have any conversation with the ascetic Gotama, ascetic?”
“I have indeed had some conversation with the ascetic Gotama, venerable sir.
“But how, Tapassī, did you have that conversation with the ascetic Gotama?
Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha-Tapassī reported to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta everything that had been the entire conversation he had with the Blessed One.
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta said this to the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī:
"Excellent, excellent, Tapassī!
Just as a learned disciple who correctly understands the Teacher’s instruction would do, so too has the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī explained it regarding the ascetic Gotama."
"For what does this wretched mental rod appear beautiful when compared with this gross bodily rod?
Indeed, the bodily rod is more blameworthy for the performance of evil action and for the occurrence of evil action than the verbal rod, and likewise than the mental rod.
When this was said, the householder Upāli said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Excellent, excellent, venerable Dīghatapassī!
Just as a learned disciple who correctly understands the Teacher’s instruction would do, so too has the venerable Tapassī explained it regarding the ascetic Gotama.
For how could this wretched mental rod compare with such a gross bodily rod?”
"Indeed, the rod of the body is far more blameworthy for the performance of evil action and for the occurrence of evil action than is the rod of speech, and so too than the rod of mind.
Come now, venerable sir, I shall go and refute the ascetic Gotama in this matter of discussion.
If the ascetic Gotama establishes himself in the same way that the venerable ascetic of great austerity has established himself;"
"Just as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by its wool and drag it, pull it, and haul it about;
even so will I drag, pull, and haul the ascetic Gotama in debate.
Just as a strong brewer’s workman might [submerge] a large brewer’s sieve in a deep pool of water..."
"Having thrown it onto a whetstone, he would take it by the ear and drag it along, pull it back and forth, and drag it all around.
In the same way, I shall drag the ascetic Gotama along, pull him back and forth, and drag him all around in debate.

Just as a powerful gambler with a drinking-bowl might take a hair by the ear and shake it, shake it out, and snap it; in the same way, I shall shake the ascetic Gotama out, shake him out thoroughly, and snap him in debate."

"Just as a sixty-year-old elephant, having plunged into a deep lotus pond, plays at a sport called 'the hemp-washer,' even so do I think I shall play the sport of 'the hemp-washer' against the ascetic Gotama.
Come now, venerable sir, I shall go and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point.
"Go then, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point."
“Either I, householder, shall refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, or Dīgha Tapassī the Nigaṇṭha, or you.
When this was said, Dīgha Tapassī the Nigaṇṭha said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Venerable sir, it does not please me that the householder Upāli should refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.”
“Venerable sir, the ascetic Gotama is a magician; he knows an alluring trick by which he entices away the disciples of other sects.
“Tapassī, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
But it is possible that the ascetic Gotama might become a disciple of the householder Upāli.”

“Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a second time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a third time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a fourth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a fifth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a sixth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a seventh time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for an eighth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a ninth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a tenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for an eleventh time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twelfth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a thirteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a fourteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a fifteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a sixteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a seventeenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for an eighteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a nineteenth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twentieth time, Dīgha Tapassī... For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twenty-first time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twenty-second time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twenty-third time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twenty-fourth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate on this very point. For either I, householder, shall challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you. And for a twenty-fifth time, Dīgha Tapassī... [repeated as above]... said: “Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate
A third time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Venerable sir, it does not please me that the householder Upāli should refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
For the ascetic Gotama, venerable sir, is a magician who knows a converting illusion by which he converts the disciples of other sects.”
“It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that the householder Upāli would become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
But it is possible that the ascetic Gotama might become a disciple of the householder Upāli.
Go, householder, and challenge the ascetic Gotama with this very point of discussion.”
“Either I, householder, shall refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, or the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, or you.
“Very well, venerable sir,” Upāli the householder replied to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having assented, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and keeping him to his right, departed for the Sārandada Mango Grove where the Blessed One was.
He approached him; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the householder Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, has the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī come here?"
“The Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī has indeed arrived here, householder.
“But did you, venerable sir, have any conversation with the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī?
“I did, householder, I had some conversation with the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī.”
“But how, venerable sir, did you have some conversation with the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī?
Then the Blessed One related to the householder Upāli everything that had been his conversation with the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī.
When this was said, the householder Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, excellent, venerable Tapassī!
Just as it should be by a learned disciple who correctly understands the Teacher’s instruction, so too has the Blessed One been answered by the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha-Tapassī.
For how could this wretched mental violence compare with such a gross physical violence?”
“Indeed, the physical rod is far more blameworthy for the performance of evil action and for the occurrence of evil action than the verbal rod, and likewise than the mental rod.
“If you, householder, were to deliberate while being established in truth, there might be a discussion between us on this matter.
“I shall deliberate, venerable sir, being established in truth.”
“Let us have a conversation on this matter.
“What do you think, householder?
Suppose here there were a Nigaṇṭha who was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, who rejected cold water and used only warm water.”
“Thus, failing to obtain cold water, he would pass away.
But where, householder, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe his rebirth?
“There are, venerable sir, gods called ‘mind-beings’ (manosattā); there he is reborn.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, he passes away bound to his mind.
“Pay attention, householder; having paid attention, householder, give your answer.”
"Indeed, what you have said later does not accord with what you said before, nor does what you said before accord with what you said later.
Yet, householder, you have spoken these words:
'Venerable sir, I shall deliberate while standing firmly on truth.'"
“Let us have a conversation on this matter.

“Venerable sir, even though the Blessed One says this, nevertheless, for the performance of evil karma and the occurrence of evil karma, the bodily rod alone is more blameworthy than the verbal rod, and more so than the mental rod.
“What do you think, householder?”

"In this case, householder, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is restrained by the fourfold restraint; he is checked by every check, yoked to every yoke, shaken off by every shaking-off, and suffused by every suffusion.
Yet as he goes forward and goes back, he brings many small living beings to destruction.
What kind of result does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe for him?"
“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta proclaims that what is unintentional is not a great offense.
“But, householder, if one intends it?
“Then, venerable sir, it becomes a great offense.”
“But regarding volition, householder, in what does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe it?
“In the mental rod, venerable sir.
“Pay attention, householder; having paid attention, householder, give your answer.”
Indeed, what you have said does not cohere: the latter with the former, nor the former with the latter.
Yet, householder, these words were spoken by you:
“Venerable sir, I shall deliberate while standing firmly on truth.”
“Let there be a conversation and discussion between us on this matter.

“Venerable sir, even though the Blessed One says this, nevertheless, for the performance of evil karma and the proceeding of evil karma, the bodily rod is indeed more blameworthy than the verbal rod, and likewise more blameworthy than the mental rod.
“What do you think, householder?”
“Is this Nāḷandā prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people?
“Yes, venerable sir, this Nāḷandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people.
“What do you think, householder?”
Suppose a man were to come here with his sword raised.
He would say:
"I shall, in a single moment, in a single instant, turn all the living beings in this Nālandā into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh."
“What do you think, householder,
would that man be able to turn all the living beings in this Nālandā into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, in a single moment, in a single instant? “Venerable sir,
even ten men, venerable sir, even twenty men, venerable sir, even thirty men, venerable sir, even forty men…”
“Venerable sir, even men possessed of wisdom, venerable sir, are not able to turn all the living beings in this Nāḷandā into a single heap of flesh,
a single mass of flesh, in a single moment, in a single instant.
For what does a single wretched man matter?”
“What do you think, householder?
Suppose a recluse or a brahmin were to come here, possessing psychic power and having attained mastery over the mind,
and he were to say this:”
‘I shall reduce this Nāḷandā to ashes with a single corruption of mind.
What do you think, householder,
would that ascetic or brahmin, possessing psychic power and attained to mastery over the mind, be able to reduce this Nāḷandā to ashes with a single corruption of mind?”

“Venerable sir, that ascetic or brahmin who possesses supernormal power and has attained mastery over his mind could reduce ten Nāḷandas, twenty Nāḷandas, thirty Nāḷandas, forty Nāḷandas, or even fifty Nāḷandas to ashes with a single corrupt thought.
For what does a single wretched Nāḷanda matter?”
“Pay attention, householder; having paid attention, householder, give your answer.
Your earlier statement does not connect with your later one, nor does your later one connect with your earlier one.
For these words were indeed spoken by you, householder:”
“Venerable sir, I shall deliberate while standing firm in truth;
let there be a discussion and exchange of views between us on this matter.

“Even though the Blessed One says this, venerable sir, nevertheless the bodily rod is far more blameworthy for the performance of evil action and for the occurrence of evil action than the verbal rod, and likewise than the mental rod.”
“What do you think, householder, have you heard that the Daṇḍaka forest,
the Kāliṅga forest, the Majjha forest, and the Mātaṅga forest were once wildernesses that became forests?
“Yes, venerable sir, I have heard that the Daṇḍaka forest, the Kāliṅga forest, the Majjha forest, and the Mātaṅga forest were once wildernesses that became forests.”
“What do you think, householder, how have you heard it? By whom was that Daṇḍaka forest, Kāliṅga forest, Majjha forest, and Mātaṅga forest turned into a wilderness, a true wilderness?
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘By the mental corruption of the seers (isīnaṃ), that Daṇḍaka forest, Kāliṅga forest, Majjha forest, and Mātaṅga forest was turned into a wilderness, a true wilderness.
“Pay attention, householder; having paid attention, householder, give your answer.”
"Indeed, what you have said later does not accord with what you said before, nor does what you said before accord with what you said later.
Yet, householder, you have spoken these words:
'Venerable sir, I shall deliberate while standing firm in truth.'"
“Let there be a conversation and discussion here with us.
“Venerable sir, I was already satisfied and delighted with the Blessed One’s first simile.
Nevertheless, desiring to hear these varied and inspired responses to questions from the Blessed One, I thought I would act in opposition to him.”
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One].”
"In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
“Investigate thoroughly, householder; thorough investigation is good for well-known people such as yourself.
“I am even more satisfied and pleased with this, Bhante, that the Blessed One says to me:
‘Investigate thoroughly, householder; thorough investigation is good for well-known people such as yourself.’”
“Venerable sir, if the followers of other sects were to gain me as a disciple, they would carry a banner all over Nāḷandā, saying:
‘The householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under us.
Yet the Blessed One says this about me:”
“Householder, investigate thoroughly; thorough investigation is good for well-known people such as yourself.
“Venerable sir, for a second time I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
“For a long time, householder, your family has been a well for the Nigaṇṭhas, such that you would think they should be given alms whenever they come to you.
“Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and pleased with the Blessed One because he says this to me:
‘For a long time, householder, your family has been a well for the Nigaṇṭhas, such that you would think they should be given alms whenever they come to you.’”
‘You should think that alms should be given even to those who have approached you.
Venerable sir, I have heard this:
‘Alms should be given to me alone; alms should not be given to others.’”
‘Alms should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others;
what is given only to me is of great fruit, not what is given to others;
what is given only to my disciples is of great fruit, not what is given to the disciples of others.’”
And yet, the Blessed One encourages me even to give gifts to the Nigaṇṭhas.
Nevertheless, venerable sir, we shall know the right time for this.
Venerable sir, for a third time I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Then the Blessed One gave the householder Upāli a graduated discourse, namely:
a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that the householder Upāli had a ready mind, a pliant mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, he then set forth that exposition of the Dhamma which is uniquely proclaimed by Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye;
In the very same way, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in the householder Upāli while he was still on that seat:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.

Then the householder Upāli, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma—having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence, and becoming independent of others in the Teacher's instruction—said this to the Blessed One:
“Now then, venerable sir, we shall depart; we have many duties and much to do.
“Then, householder, you may go at your own convenience.
Then the householder Upāli, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and [departed] from the Blessed One.
Having paid homage and circumambulated him, he went to his own residence. Upon arrival, he addressed the gatekeeper:
"From this day forward, my dear gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs, but I leave the door open for the Blessed One, the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.
If any Nigaṇṭha comes, you should say this to him:"
“Stop, venerable sir; do not enter.
From this day forward, the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.
The door is closed to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs, but it is open to the Blessed One’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”
“If you need almsfood, venerable sir, stay right here; they will bring it to you right here.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the doorkeeper replied to the householder Upāli.
Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī heard:
“It is said, householder Upāli has gone over to discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.
Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“I have heard this, venerable sir: it is said that the householder Upāli has gone over to discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.”
“It is impossible, Tapassī, it is out of the question that the householder Upāli could become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
But it is possible that the ascetic Gotama might become a disciple of the householder Upāli.
A second time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha-Tapassī said: “… [as before] …”
A third time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“I have heard this, venerable sir… [as before]….”
“...might enter into discipleship under the householder Upāli.
“In that case, Bhante, I shall go to find out whether or not the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.
“Go then, Tapassī, and find out whether or not the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.”
Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī approached the residence of the householder Upāli.
The doorkeeper saw the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī coming from afar,
and having seen him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Dīghatapassī:
“Stop, venerable sir; do not enter.
From this day forward, the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.
The door is closed to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs, but it is open to the Blessed One’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”
“If you need almsfood, venerable sir, stay right here; they will bring it to you right here.
“I have no need for almsfood, friend,” he said, and turning back from there, he approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. Having approached him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“It is indeed true, venerable sir, that the householder Upāli has gone over to discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.”
“Indeed, Bhante, I did not succeed in persuading you. Bhante, it does not please me that the householder Upāli should challenge the ascetic Gotama to a debate.
For the ascetic Gotama, Bhante, is a magician who knows a converting illusion by which he converts the disciples of other sects.
Bhante, the householder Upāli has been converted by the ascetic Gotama through his converting illusion.”
“It is impossible, Tapassī, it is out of the question that the householder Upāli could become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
But it is quite possible that the ascetic Gotama might become a disciple of the householder Upāli.
For a second time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha-Tapassī said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“It is indeed true, venerable sir...
[as before] ...I would enter into discipleship under the householder Upāli.
For a third time, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Indeed, Bhante, it would be the truth...
[as before] ...that I would enter into discipleship under the householder Upāli.”
“Come now, Tapassī, I shall go so that I may know for myself whether or not the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama.
Then the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas, approached the residence of the householder Upāli.
The doorkeeper saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
"Stop, venerable sir, do not enter.
From this day forward, the householder Upāli has entered into discipleship under the ascetic Gotama."
“The door is closed for the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs, but it is open for the Blessed One, the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.
If you need almsfood, venerable sir, stay right here; they will bring it to you.
“In that case, my good gatekeeper, go to the householder Upāli; having approached him, speak thus to the householder Upāli:”
“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is standing outside the gatehouse together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas;
he wishes to see you.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the doorkeeper replied to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and having approached the householder Upāli, he said this to him:
“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is standing outside the outer gate together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas;
he wishes to see you.
“In that case, my good doorkeeper, prepare seats in the middle hall.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the doorkeeper replied to the householder Upāli. Having arranged seats in the middle gatehouse, he approached the householder Upāli and said to him:
“Venerable sir, the seats have been prepared in the middle gatehouse.
Now, please do as you deem fit.”
Then the householder Upāli went to the middle gate-hall; having arrived, he sat down himself upon the seat there that was foremost, best, supreme, and most excellent, and addressed the doorkeeper:
"In that case, my good doorkeeper, go to where the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta is; having approached him, say this to the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta:
'Venerable sir, the householder Upāli says thus—'"
“Please enter, venerable sir, if you so desire.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the gatekeeper replied to the householder Upāli, and he approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. Having approached him, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Venerable sir, the householder Upāli says this:”
“Enter, venerable sir, if you so desire.
Then the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas, approached the middle gate-hall.
Then the householder Upāli—
Whenever he previously saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming from afar, having seen him,
he would go out to meet him and, having swept and prepared with his upper robe the seat there that was foremost, best, supreme, and most excellent, he would have him sit upon it.
Then, having sat down himself on the seat there that was foremost, best, supreme, and most excellent, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
"Venerable sir, there are seats available;
if you wish, please sit."
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said this to the householder Upāli:
“You are mad, householder! You are demented, householder!
Having gone with the thought, ‘Venerable sir, I shall refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine,’ you have returned bound by a great net of arguments.”

“Householder, it is just as if a man who goes out to remove eggs were to return with the eggs already removed; or again, householder, it is as if a man who goes out to remove eyes were to return with his eyes already removed.
In the same way, householder, you set out thinking, ‘Venerable sir, I shall go and refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine,’ but you have returned bound by a great snare of arguments.
You have been ensnared, householder, by the ascetic Gotama with his ensnaring illusion.”
“Venerable sir, this is a charming illusion;
venerable sir, this is a lovely illusion.
Venerable sir, my beloved kinsmen and blood relatives might be drawn back by this illusion; it would lead to the welfare and happiness of those beloved kinsmen and blood relatives for a long time.”

"Venerable sir, if all the khattiyas were to be turned back by this turning-back, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of those khattiyas for a long time. Venerable sir, if all the brahmins... [and so on] ...the vessas...
[and so on] ...the suddas were to be turned back by this turning-back, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of those suddas for a long time."
"Venerable sir, even if the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,

its devas and humans, were to be turned back by this turning-back formula, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of that world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, for a long time."
"In that case, venerable sir, I shall give you a simile;
for by means of a simile some wise men understand the meaning of what has been said.
Once upon a time, venerable sir, a certain brahmin who was aged, elderly, and advanced in years had a young wife who was pregnant and near her confinement."
Then, Bhante, that young woman said this to the brahmin:
“Go, brahmin, buy a young monkey from the market and bring it back; it will be a plaything for my boy.
When this was said, the brahmin said this to the young woman:
“Wait a moment, madam, until she has given birth.
If you give birth to a boy, madam, I will go to the market, buy a young male monkey, and bring it back for you to be a plaything for the boy.
But if you give birth to a girl, madam, I will go to the market, buy a young female monkey, and bring it back for you to be a plaything for the girl.”
A second time, venerable sir, that young woman...
[and] a third time, venerable sir, that young woman said this to that brahmin:
"Go, brahmin, buy a young monkey from the market and bring it back; it will be a plaything for my boy."
Then, venerable sir, that brahmin, being infatuated with and bound by his heart to that young woman, bought a young male monkey from the market and brought it back, saying to her:
"Madam, this young male monkey has been bought from the market and brought here for you; it will be a plaything for your little boy.
When this was said, venerable sir, that young woman said this to the brahmin:
“Go, brahmin, take this young monkey and go to where Rattapāṇi, the dyer’s son, is; having approached him, say to Rattapāṇi the dyer’s son:
‘Friend Rattapāṇi, I wish for this young monkey to be dyed with the dye called Pītāvalepana, washed and re-washed until it is smooth on both sides.
Then, venerable sir, that brahmin, infatuated and his mind bound to that young woman, took that young monkey...
Taking it, he approached the dyer’s son Rattapāṇi. Having approached him, he said this to the dyer’s son Rattapāṇi:
“Friend Rattapāṇi, I wish to have this young monkey dyed with a dye called ‘yellow ointment,’ pounded and re-pounded, and rubbed smooth on both sides.
When this was said, venerable sir, the dyer’s son Rattapāṇi said this to that brahmin:
“‘Venerable sir, this young monkey is indeed capable of taking dye, but it is not capable of withstanding beating, nor is it capable of withstanding rubbing.

In the same way, venerable sir, the doctrine of the foolish Nigaṇṭhas is indeed capable of taking dye among the foolish, but not among the wise; it is not capable of withstanding inquiry, nor is it capable of withstanding rubbing.
Then, venerable sir, on another occasion that brahmin took a pair of new cloths and approached Rattapāṇi the dyer’s son; having approached him, he said this to Rattapāṇi the dyer’s son:
“I wish, friend Rattapāṇi, to have this new pair of cloths dyed in the dye called yellow-ointment, pounded and re-pounded, and smoothed on both sides.
When this was said, venerable sir, the dyer’s son Rattapāṇi said to that brahmin:
“This new pair of cloths of yours, venerable sir, is indeed capable of taking dye, capable of being pounded, and capable of being smoothed.”

“In the same way, venerable sir, the doctrine of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is acceptable to the wise and not to the foolish; it is capable of being examined and capable of being analyzed.
“Householder, the assembly, including the king, knows this:
‘The householder Upāli is a disciple of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.’”
“Householder, whose disciple do you consider me to be?

When this was said, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, he said this to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“In that case, venerable sir, listen as to whose disciple I am.”
“For the steadfast one, free from delusion,
who has shattered his impurity and conquered all victory;
for him who is free from affliction and whose mind is perfectly composed— ”
Of him who has grown in virtue, who possesses noble wisdom,
who dwells in solitude, and who is stainless—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One.
For the one free from doubt, contented,
who has cast off worldly bait and rejoices,
for that person who has accomplished the life of a recluse—
Of that Blessed One, whose final body has been cast off, who is incomparable and free from passion, I am a disciple.
To the one free from doubt, the skilled,
the discipliner, the supreme charioteer,
the unsurpassed one of radiant Dhamma—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One— the one free from doubt, the illuminator, the hero who cuts through conceit.
Of the peerless, the immeasurable,
the profound, who has attained silence,
the maker of security, the knower—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who is established in the Dhamma, restrained, transcended attachment, and liberated.
To the Naga who dwells in the forest,
whose fetters are destroyed and who is liberated,
the one who has shaken off defilements and is a master of reflection—
Of him who has lowered the banner, who is free from passion,
who is tamed and beyond conceptual proliferation—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One.
Of one who has attained the sevenfold wisdom, who is free from deceit, who possesses the three knowledges, who has reached the state of a Brahmā,
who is purified, and who is a master of the verses.
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, the Sakka who bestows gifts first, who is tranquil and has known what is to be known.
Of the Noble One whose self is developed,
who has attained the goal, the expounder,
the mindful one, the possessor of insight—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who does not bend forward nor lean back, who is unshakable, and has attained mastery.
For one who has risen up, who meditates,
whose mind is not followed by others, who is pure,
who is unattached, and who is beneficial—
To him who is secluded and has reached the pinnacle,
who has crossed over and is ferrying others across—
to that Blessed One, I am a disciple.
Of the peaceful one, of vast wisdom,
of great insight, and free from greed—
the Tathāgata, the Sugata.
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who is peerless, incomparable, confident, and subtle.
To the Buddha who has severed craving,
who is smokeless and unstained,
the Yakṣa worthy of offerings—
“I am a disciple of that Blessed One, the supreme person, the incomparable, who has attained the pinnacle of great glory.”
“But when, householder, were these praises of the ascetic Gotama uttered by you?
“Just as if, venerable sir, there were a great heap of various flowers, and a skilled garland-maker or a garland-maker’s apprentice were to weave them into a variegated garland—
just so, venerable sir, is that Blessed One many-colored, possessing many hundreds of colors.”
“Who indeed, Bhante, would not praise one who is worthy of praise?
Then, unable to endure the Blessed One’s honor, hot blood gushed from the mouth of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta right there.
The Upāli Sutta, the sixth, is finished.
